claims.title: Palladius sent to the Irish
claims.summary: Pope Celestine I commissioned the bishop Palladius as the first bishop 'to the Irish believing in Christ', marking the formal arrival of organised Christianity on the island.

sources.label: Ireland Converts to Christianity

claims.title: The mission of St Patrick
claims.summary: The British-born missionary Patrick, traditionally active from the 430s, evangelised much of Ireland, secured toleration for Christians and fostered a native clergy and monasticism; his feast is 17 March.

claims.title: Columba founds Iona
claims.summary: The Irish monk Columba established the monastery of Iona off western Scotland, a launching point for the spread of Christianity and Irish learning into Scotland and Northumbria.

claims.title: The monastic golden age
claims.summary: Monasteries such as Clonard, Clonmacnoise and Bangor became renowned centres of learning whose scribes copied Western literature and produced illuminated manuscripts, while Irish missionaries evangelised Europe.

claims.summary: Scandinavian raiders struck Rathlin Island in 795, beginning decades of assaults on the rich coastal monasteries recorded with alarm in the Irish annals.

claims.title: Founding of Dublin as a longphort
claims.summary: The Vikings built a fortified ship-camp (longphort) at Dublin in 841 and overwintered there, founding what would become Ireland's most important town and a hub of Norse trade.

claims.title: Brian Boru becomes High King
claims.summary: Brian Boru of the Dál Cais of Munster made himself High King of Ireland around 1002, the most powerful ruler the island had known and a claimant to authority over all of Ireland.

claims.summary: On Good Friday 1014 Brian Boru's army defeated the Norse of Dublin and the men of Leinster near Dublin, breaking Viking political power in Ireland; Brian was killed in the battle.

claims.title: Anglo-Norman landing in Ireland
claims.summary: At the invitation of the exiled Leinster king Diarmait Mac Murchada, Anglo-Norman, Welsh and Flemish forces landed in Wexford in 1169, beginning centuries of English involvement in Ireland.

claims.title: Henry II and the Lordship of Ireland
claims.summary: Henry II landed at Waterford in 1171, the first English king in Ireland, and established the Lordship of Ireland; in 1177 he made his son John 'Lord of Ireland'.

claims.title: The Nine Years' War and the Battle of Kinsale
claims.summary: The Ulster lords Hugh O'Neill and Hugh Roe O'Donnell led a war against Elizabethan rule with Spanish support; at Kinsale on Christmas Eve 1601 (3 January 1602 by the new calendar) their army was routed by Lord Deputy Mountjoy, and the war ended in 1603.

claims.title: Scottish settlement of Antrim and Down
claims.summary: The private settlement of the Ayrshire Scots James Hamilton and Hugh Montgomery brought hundreds of Scottish families to north Down from 1606, and others settled in Antrim; these two counties lay outside the official Plantation of Ulster.

sources.label: The Plantation: When?
The Ulster Plantation

claims.title: Flight of the Earls and the Plantation of Ulster
claims.summary: After the Gaelic earls sailed from Rathmullan in September 1607, King James I planted English and Scottish Protestant settlers on confiscated lands in six Ulster counties (Armagh, Cavan, Coleraine, Donegal, Fermanagh and Tyrone) from 1609, embedding a lasting religious and political division.

claims.title: Cromwellian conquest
claims.summary: Oliver Cromwell's parliamentary army stormed Drogheda and Wexford with notorious massacres; the conquest was followed by the 1652 Act for the Settlement of Ireland and the mass confiscation of Catholic land.

claims.title: Williamite victory and the Penal era
claims.summary: The Protestant William III defeated the Catholic James II at the Boyne in 1690 and Limerick in 1691, after which the Protestant Ascendancy entrenched its rule through the anti-Catholic Penal Laws.

sources.publisher: John J. Burns Library, Boston College

claims.title: Act of Union
claims.summary: The Act of Union merged the Kingdom of Ireland with Great Britain into the United Kingdom on 1 January 1801, abolishing the Irish Parliament and placing Ireland under direct rule from Westminster.

sources.label: Charles Stewart Parnell and the Home Rule Movement
sources.publisher: University of Delaware Library (Easter Rising exhibition)

claims.title: The Great Famine (An Gorta Mór)
claims.summary: Potato blight destroyed Ireland's staple crop from 1845; about a million people died and a million more emigrated, and the population fell sharply even as food continued to be exported amid an inadequate British relief effort.

sources.label: Irish Potato Famine: Date, Cause & Great Hunger

claims.title: The Land League and the Land War
claims.summary: The Irish National Land League, founded in 1879 with Charles Stewart Parnell as president, mobilised tenant farmers against landlordism, opening the 'Land War' over rents and ownership.

sources.label: Charles Stewart Parnell and the Home Rule Movement
sources.publisher: University of Delaware Library (Easter Rising exhibition)

claims.title: The Home Rule bills
claims.summary: Under Parnell's pressure the Liberal government introduced Home Rule bills in 1886 and 1893 to give Ireland self-government within the UK; both were defeated, but Home Rule became the central Irish demand.

sources.label: Charles Stewart Parnell and the Home Rule Movement
sources.publisher: University of Delaware Library (Easter Rising exhibition)

claims.summary: Against the third Home Rule Bill, 471,414 people signed Ulster's Solemn League and Covenant or, in the case of women, the Declaration, pledging to use 'all means which may be found necessary' to defeat a Home Rule parliament in Dublin.

claims.title: Home Rule enacted and suspended
claims.summary: The third Home Rule Bill received Royal Assent as the Government of Ireland Act 1914, but a Suspensory Act passed alongside it suspended its operation for the duration of the First World War; it never came into effect.

claims.title: The Easter Rising
claims.summary: Republicans seized the General Post Office and other Dublin sites and proclaimed an Irish Republic; the rising was suppressed within a week, but the execution of its leaders turned opinion towards independence.

sources.label: Irish History Timeline – From 1916 to Today

claims.title: Sinn Féin's general election victory
claims.summary: In the December 1918 general election Sinn Féin won 73 of Ireland's 105 Westminster seats; its elected members refused to sit in London and constituted themselves as the first Dáil in Dublin.

sources.label: The 1918 General Election in Ireland
sources.publisher: ARK, Queen's University Belfast and Ulster University

claims.title: War of Independence
claims.summary: After Sinn Féin's 1918 victory and the first Dáil in 1919, the IRA waged a guerrilla war against British forces until a truce on 11 July 1921 opened the way to negotiations.

sources.label: Irish History Timeline – From 1916 to Today

claims.title: Government of Ireland Act: six counties
claims.summary: The Act created two Home Rule parliaments and defined Northern Ireland as the six counties of Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry and Tyrone. In March 1920 the Ulster Unionist Council had rejected a nine-county Ulster, which the 1911 census showed to be only about 56 per cent Protestant, as bringing an anti-unionist representation strong enough to endanger a northern parliament, leaving Cavan, Donegal and Monaghan to the south.

claims.title: Anglo-Irish Treaty
claims.summary: The Treaty signed in London created the Irish Free State as a dominion within the British Empire; under its Article 12 Northern Ireland, already established by the Government of Ireland Act 1920, could opt out within a month, and a Boundary Commission would then determine the border.

claims.title: Civil War over the Treaty
claims.summary: The Treaty split the movement: pro-Treaty forces under Michael Collins fought anti-Treaty republicans under Éamon de Valera in a civil war that the Free State won at heavy cost.

claims.summary: The Irish Free State formally came into being on 6 December 1922; the following afternoon the Parliament of Northern Ireland decided to exercise its right under the Treaty to remain outside it.

claims.title: Boundary Commission report suppressed
claims.summary: After the Morning Post revealed in November 1925 that the Treaty's Boundary Commission would propose only a minor two-way transfer of territory, the British, Free State and Northern Ireland governments agreed to revoke Article 12 and confirm the existing border; the report was suppressed and published only in 1969.

claims.title: A new Constitution claims the whole island
claims.summary: Bunreacht na hÉireann, enacted by referendum on 1 July 1937, came into operation; its Article 2 declared that the national territory 'consists of the whole island of Ireland', a claim replaced in 1999 under the Good Friday Agreement.

claims.title: Declaration of the Republic
claims.summary: The Republic of Ireland Act, signed 21 December 1948 and in force from 18 April 1949, declared the twenty-six-county state a republic, removed the King's last role and left the Commonwealth.

claims.summary: British Royal Marines landed on the uninhabited Atlantic islet of Rockall in 1955 and claimed it for the United Kingdom; it was declared part of Scotland by the Island of Rockall Act 1972.

claims.title: Derry civil rights march and the start of the Troubles
claims.summary: The RUC baton-charged a civil rights march in Derry, scenes broadcast worldwide; the day is widely regarded as the beginning of the Troubles. Of the 3,532 deaths the Sutton Index records from 1969 to 2001, republican paramilitaries caused 58 per cent, loyalist paramilitaries 29 per cent and the British security forces 10 per cent.

claims.title: Bloody Sunday
claims.summary: British soldiers shot dead 13 civilians on a civil rights march in Derry and wounded others, one of whom later died; the Saville Inquiry found in 2010 that none of the casualties was posing a threat of causing death or serious injury, and the Prime Minister called the killings 'unjustified and unjustifiable'.

claims.summary: The IRA planted and exploded 22 bombs across Belfast in the space of 75 minutes, killing nine people and seriously injuring about 130.

claims.summary: After a 1972 referendum carried by over 80 per cent, Ireland joined the European Economic Community on 1 January 1973, beginning a transformation from an agricultural economy to a modern European state.

claims.summary: Four car bombs in Dublin and Monaghan killed 33 civilians and an unborn child. claims.summary: The 1998 Agreement settled the conflict over Northern Ireland on the principle of consent and created power-sharing institutions; Ireland amended Articles 2 and 3 of its Constitution to replace its territorial claim with a peaceful aspiration to unity.

claims.summary: A car bomb claimed by the Real IRA, a group opposed to the IRA ceasefire, killed 29 people in Omagh, among them nine children and a woman pregnant with twins: the greatest loss of life in any single incident of the conflict, months after the Good Friday Agreement.

claims.title: Census: more of Catholic than Protestant background
claims.summary: Northern Ireland's 2021 census, published in 2022, counted 45.7 per cent of residents as Catholic by current religion or upbringing and 43.5 per cent as Protestant or other Christian, against 45.1 and 48.4 per cent in 2011; 9.3 per cent had no religion either way.

claims.title: First nationalist First Minister
claims.summary: Power-sharing was restored two years after the DUP left the Executive over post-Brexit trade arrangements, and Sinn Féin's Michelle O'Neill became the first nationalist First Minister of Northern Ireland, alongside the DUP's Emma Little-Pengelly as deputy First Minister.
